newsitem.title: FRANCE: Fly the French flag against far-right - Juppe.
newsitem.headline: Fly the French flag against far-right - Juppe.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, linking Jean-Marie Le Pen's National Front to Nazi collaborators, urged fellow Gaullists on Monday to fly the flag of patriotism against the extreme right.

Marking the 50th anniversary of the Gaullist movement in Strasbourg, where anti-immigration crusader Le Pen claimed last week to be the heir to General Charles de Gaulle, Juppe urged mainstream conservatives to reassert their national colours.

"Let us not allow the tricolor flag and the symbols of our history to be monopolised by those who who are nostalgic for the people who in 1940 gave France a caricature of fascism and capitulation," he told a rally of the Gaullist RPR party.
"For us, the foundation stone of Gaullism is love of our homeland. Let us, as proud Gaullists, make patriotism our flag," Juppe declared.

Amid speculation that President Jacques Chirac, founder of the present-day Gaullist party, could bring forward a general election due next March, Juppe urged Gaullists to be the driving force of national unity in the face of "professionals of demagoguery, hatred and scandal".
France's national destiny was now linked to Europe, he said.
Le Pen regularly accuses the political establishment of selling out France's national identity to the European Union.

Amid labour unrest over austerity to meet the criteria for joining the single European currency, Juppe said Paris had to find a balance between the demands of international economic competition and social rules ensuring the nation's cohesion.

He also said Gaullists had to be morally worthy of public trust, responding to Le Pen's accusations of corruption against establishment parties mired in scandals over alleged illicit campaign funding.

Some 1,000 Gaullist dignitaries celebrated the founding of the first postwar Gaullist party in 1947 in the same conference hall where Le Pen's party, which has grown to 15 percent national support, held a controversial Easter weekend congress against a backdrop of mass left-wing protests.
The RPR has singled out Le Pen as a target in the forthcoming election but stayed away from the Strasbourg protests, saying they only served to give Le Pen publicity.

The leader of the Gaullists' UDF centrist coalition partner, ex-defence minister Francois Leotard, sparked anger last month by equating extreme-right and the Socialist-led parliamentary opposition as adversaries.

De Gaulle, leader of Free France in opposition to Nazi Germany during World War Two, founded the French People's Rally (RPF) in Strasbourg in 1947 after leaving power in disgust at the revolving-door party politics of the Fourth Republic.
When he returned to power in 1958, the party was transformed into the Union of Democrats for the Republic (UDR), which dominated government until 1974.
Chirac refounded it again in 1976 as the Rally for the Republic (RPR).
